summary: This informational document captures the design rationale of the early draft that became RFC 8205, the BGPsec protocol specification. It lists the decisions made for and against each design choice along with the supporting discussion. It gives background on why BGPsec looks the way it does.

eli5.summary: When a team builds something, it helps to write down why they chose each part. This is that diary for the internet route-signing system.

questions: why was bgpsec designed this way
what design choices were made for bgpsec
what signature algorithm does bgpsec use
subtitle: Design decisions for route signing in Border Gateway Protocol.

tldr.problem: BGP, the Internet's routing protocol, has no built-in protection against forged or modified routing announcements. An attacker can inject false routes or alter the path through which traffic flows.
tldr.mechanism: BGPsec adds cryptographic signatures to routing announcements so that routers can verify that each AS in the path actually authorized the route and that the path has not been tampered with. This RFC explains the design decisions made to achieve this protection while keeping deployment practical.
tldr.outcome: BGPsec (RFC 8205) provides full autonomous system path validation. This design document captures the rationale behind key choices: using ECDSA-P256 signatures, signing only certain attributes, requiring transport security for withdrawals, and supporting incremental deployment alongside traditional BGP.

facts.label: Signature algorithm
facts.value: ECDSA with curve P-256 and SHA-256

today: RFC 8374 is an Informational RFC that documents the design rationale of BGPsec (RFC 8205). BGPsec is still in early deployment stages as a security enhancement to BGP routing.

sections.title: BGPsec Goals and Design Context
sections.content:
BGP (Border Gateway Protocol) is the protocol routers use to announce which networks they can reach. The problem is that BGP has no built-in security: any router can claim to reach any network, and the routing system will believe it. An attacker can hijack traffic by announcing false routes.

BGPsec adds cryptographic signatures to routing announcements so routers can verify them. The protocol has four high-level goals: rigorous path validation for all prefixes, incremental deployment (no flag-day requirement), protection of inter-domain (eBGP) paths only, and preservation of privacy (no disclosure of peering relations). This RFC explains the design decisions made to achieve these goals, such as why certain attributes are signed and others are not, what cryptographic algorithms to use, and how to manage the transition from unsigned BGP to signed BGPsec.
sections.eli5: BGP lets routers tell each other which networks they can reach. BGPsec adds digital signatures so routers can verify that an announcement really came from the network it claims to be from.

sections.title: Cryptographic Foundations
sections.content:
BGPsec uses Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm (ECDSA) with curve P-256 and SHA-256 hashing for signing routing announcements. This choice was made because ECDSA P-256 produces smaller signatures (256 bits) compared to RSA-2048 (2048 bits), keeping BGP update messages and router memory tables smaller.

Each BGPsec router within an AS has its own unique key pair, represented by a certificate in the Resource Public Key Infrastructure (RPKI). If a router is compromised, its key can be revoked independently without affecting other routers in the same AS. During transitions from one signature algorithm to the next, updates will carry two sets of signatures (two Signature_Blocks), one for each algorithm, allowing routers to validate against either algorithm during the changeover period (expected to last 2 to 4 years).
sections.eli5: Each router signs announcements with its own key, like a personal signature on a letter. If a router gets hacked, its key can be disabled without affecting other routers.

sections.title: Path Signatures and What Gets Signed
sections.content:
The originating AS (the one announcing a prefix) signs the Network Layer Reachability Information (NLRI) prefix, its own AS number, the next AS number in the path, and the signature algorithm suite ID. Each upstream AS along the path then signs the previous AS's signature along with the next AS number—a method chosen to minimize the amount of data being hashed (keeping performance efficient) while still securing the entire path.

Notably, not all BGP attributes are signed. Withdrawal messages are not signed because BGPsec assumes transport-layer security between neighboring routers; an external attacker cannot inject fake withdrawals. Attributes like Local_Pref and Community are also unsigned because they are local to each router and do not need inter-domain protection. This design choice balances security with the reality that not everything needs cryptographic protection.
sections.eli5: Each router signs a receipt saying what it saw from the router before it. That way, if someone tampers with the path, the signature breaks.

sections.title: Incremental Deployment and Coexistence
sections.content:
One of BGPsec's key design goals is incremental deployment: the ability to roll out BGPsec without requiring all routers to upgrade at once. BGP signatures are carried in a new optional, non-transitive attribute, so routers that do not understand BGPsec can ignore the signatures and still process the routes. This allows traditional BGP and BGPsec to coexist.

During deployment, operators face choices about whether to support partial path signing (where only some ASes in a path have upgraded to BGPsec), whether certain stub ASes with limited resources can use proxy signing (having another AS sign on their behalf), and how to handle multiple peering sessions between the same pair of ASes. The RFC documents these considerations so operators can make informed decisions that fit their network topology and constraints.
sections.eli5: Not every router needs to be upgraded at the same time. Old routers and new routers can work together during the switchover.

sections.title: Optimization and Operational Trade-Offs
sections.content:
BGPsec introduces several operational design choices made to balance security, efficiency, and deployability. Each BGPsec update carries only one prefix (not multiple), because if an upstream AS chose to propagate only some prefixes from an update, the signatures would break. This imposes a performance cost (more updates to process) to preserve security and the normal level of route information exposure.

Interaction with common BGP features such as peer groups, confederations, and route servers in Internet exchange points are considered, and the design accommodates these features. The RFC also addresses what happens when signatures fail validation: unsigned updates from partially upgraded routers are processed according to defined rules, and syntactic errors in signatures are handled carefully to avoid breaking the flow of legitimate traffic during transition periods.
sections.eli5: Some design choices make BGPsec updates larger or more frequent, but they are necessary to keep signatures valid and to let the protocol work with features routers already use.
